title: Detachment in the home
hookLine: why go searching in the forest? the ninth Guru finds the One in the house

cards: Seven in the morning. Lunches half packed, a kettle starting to whistle, someone who can't find a shoe, a phone buzzing on the counter. In the back of the mind runs an old idea: the real spiritual life is elsewhere.
On a mountain, in a forest, in a quiet room where no one asks where the shoe is. Guru Tegh Bahadur had a family: a wife, Mata Gujri, and a son who would become the tenth Guru.
He had a household, a sangat, and plenty of people asking him for things. And he wrote a hymn that begins with a question about that forest.

teach.b: The hymn is in Raga Dhanasri, paraphrased. Why go searching for Him in the forest? He dwells in all, always untouched, and He lives with you too.

teach.h: FRAGRANCE IN A FLOWER, A FACE IN A MIRROR.
teach.b: Then two pictures: like the fragrance that lives in a flower, like the reflection that lives in a mirror. So He dwells within; search inside, brother. Look closely.
The fragrance is all through the flower, but you can't pick it out and hold it. The reflection is in the mirror, but the mirror isn't stained by it.

Present, and untouched, at the same time. That's the hymn's word for the One: alepa, unstained, unclinging. And if the One can live in everything without clinging, a person can live in a house the same way.
That's what detachment means here. It isn't leaving, or caring less about the people at the breakfast table.
It's loving the home without being owned by it: packing the lunch with full attention, and not falling apart when the day goes sideways.

Tradition says Guru Tegh Bahadur spent long stretches in quiet remembrance at Bakala before the Guruship came to him; back in year one, a trader found him there. But quiet didn't mean leaving his family.
He stayed a householder, and the hymn points the same way. It doesn't scorn the forest. It says the search can begin at home.
Held lightly, a home doesn't get smaller. It gets roomier, with space for the kettle, the lost shoe, and the One who, the Guru says, was there the whole time.

how: Sikhs follow the Gurus in living as householders, keeping family and work while remembering the Name, rather than renouncing the world; this hymn of Guru Tegh Bahadur is sung in kirtan on that theme.

games.q: what does “detachment in the home” mean?
o: keeping your feelings for family at a cool distance
leaving home to seek God alone in the forest
loving family fully without being owned by it

games.q: the hymn's pictures: tap the pairs.
p: all through it, never picked out
where the hymn says you needn't go

s: detachment in this hymn means leaving your family
the Guru stayed a householder; the hymn says the One already lives with you.
the hymn asks why anyone would search for the One in the forest
He dwells in all, and lives with you too.
in the hymn, the mirror is stained by the reflection
the reflection is present and the mirror stays untouched; that's the picture of detachment.

games.q: the house is loud, the days are full, and you long to leave it all for a quiet forest to find God. what does the ninth Guru's hymn say?
o: go: the real search is in the wild.
stay, and search within: He already lives with you.
give up searching until the kids are grown.
games.why: why go searching in the forest? He dwells in all and lives with you, like fragrance in a flower. search inside.

practice: Walk through your home in your mind, room by room, and in each one notice a person or a thing you love there, letting the love be full.
Then, on the breath out, let it rest there without grasping, the way a mirror holds a face and keeps no stain. If you pray, remember Waheguru as present in each room.

wordCard.voice: Detachment in the home. Living fully with family and work, like fragrance in a flower, present everywhere and clinging to nothing. Today's word.

orig.note: untouched, unstained; the hymn's word for the One who dwells in all and clings to nothing.

carryVoice: Your line: home, held lightly. Full love, and no stain. Go gently.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Dhanasri Mahala 9, Ang 684 (kahe re ban khojan jaee: fragrance in the flower, reflection in the mirror)
